speaker: chrisshook
text: I'll go ahead and mute. Well, thank you, Deputy Chief. I appreciate that. And then the last agenda item that we have is the appeal process overview. And I'm going to keep this relatively short. Each member here of the board has a copy of the ordinance, and that sets it out pretty clearly what the process looks like. And so if you have any questions at all, you can reach out to me about that process. But at its core, your jurisdiction is essentially a pellet. The complaint process begins, and I'm going to try and share my screen again. There's your schedule. Okay. Now the complaint process begins when a citizen files a complaint with the division of police. And that citizen alleges that a police officer engaged in conduct that discriminated against that citizen for one of the reasons that we talked about earlier. The initial complaint is investigated by the police department. It's typically investigated by one of the lieutenants in the police department, and they will issue findings and recommendations to the chief. If the chief, after reviewing the findings and recommendations from the internal investigation, determines that the complaint has no merit or only has merit in part, the chief will inform the complainant, who will then have the ability to appeal that determination directly to you, the civilian review board. And at that point, the case will get transmitted directly to the board. And the responsibility of beginning the conduct of appellate investigation will fall to the chair of the board in consultation with my office. As part of the appellate process, you have the right to receive a full copy of the case file, which includes police reports, videos, whether cruiser videos or body-worn cameras, and internal investigation investigator notes. You can request additional evidence that you might think might be appropriate. Notice is provided to both the complainant, the person making that appeal to the board, and also to the officer or officers who are the subject of the complaint. And then the matter gets set for a hearing that would take place before the board. There has been some discussion about subpoena power. The board does have some subpoena power. You can require the attendance of certain witnesses, the production of certain documents. The board does not, however, have the power to subpoena an individual officer. That responsibility falls to the supervisory officers in the police department who direct their officers to appear and testify before the board. We've had a lot of discussions, both with the supervisory personnel in the police department, our rank and file officers, and with the fraternal order of police about how we expect that process to go. If we find that we are having difficulties with cooperation on that, that is, again, one of those issues that can come back before counsel to review whether to give the review board subpoena power at that time. The hearing process is that it operates very much like a trial. So for the attorneys here on the board, you probably have a pretty strong understanding of what that looks like. But for everyone else, this is, the hearing process is about receiving the evidence that would either support or refute the appeal from the complainant, listening to testimony from witnesses, having those witnesses be subject to potential cross-examination, either by an attorney for the complainant, to which they are entitled, or an attorney for the officer, to which they are entitled, or questions that may be presented by either myself or from individual members of the board. After receiving the evidence, the board members will be able to deliberate. Deliberations of the board as a quasi-judicial body are not required to be in an open meeting. So you are able to deliberate your findings in private. Once we are able to do meetings in person, again, we do have a city council conference room where that is quite appropriate for deliberations and should provide enough space for each member to engage in those deliberations. During your deliberations, you are, the findings that you are able to reach fall under four different categories. One category is sustained. So if you were to find by a preponderance of the evidence that the conduct of the officer was discriminatory towards the complainant, then you would issue a sustained finding. Conversely, if you were to find by a preponderance of the evidence that the officer's actions were consistent with division of police policy, procedure, and training, you would issue a finding of exonerated. If you were to find that the alleged conduct did not occur, and this is a little bit different from exoneration, this would mean that essentially there was no basis for the complainant to have presented what they presented, you would issue what we call an unfounded finding. And that is only slightly different than an exonerated finding. And then finally, if you were to find that neither the complainant nor the evidence in support of the officer's position were more likely than not to support one side of the other, you would issue a finding of insufficient evidence. Now, those findings that you make and those votes would take place in an open meeting. And then the final summary would be prepared by the board chair in consultation with my office and then represented to the board for a vote. One thing I want to be clear about, and Mr. Christie probably understands this as well as anybody, if he has worked with the Fraternal Order of Police before in negotiations, is that we do have a contract with our police officers. They are members of a union, the Fraternal Order of Police. And consequently, we have a collective bargaining agreement. As part of that collective bargaining agreement, the final decision about whether an officer violated a policy that would subject them to discipline, that final decision has to rest with the chief of police and with the mayor. So the final summary, let's say the board were to issue a sustained finding. That would get presented to the mayor and the chief of police, and then they would make a determination based upon their review of that final summary, whether they agree with it and whether they are going to issue their own finding that the officer violated policy. And then if they make that decision, they can move on to discipline. I know that in a lot of public discussion about civilian review boards, not just here in Reynoldsburg, but in other communities and probably most prominently in Columbus, there's been a lot of discussion about giving the review boards the ability to make binding findings and to recommend discipline or to impose discipline. With our current collective bargaining agreement with the Fraternal Order of Police, we could not give this board that kind of power or we would have been in breach of that agreement. It is important for us to maintain our contractual obligations to our union police officers in the collective bargaining process. But what this process most assuredly does is that it provides transparency. When these complaints are made, there are internal investigations conducted and most of the time the public never hears about any of that, the findings, the investigation process itself. This is a process by which we are able to bring that out into the open, into an open meeting and give members of the community the ability to be able to review that information and to be able to provide their intelligent and learned opinion to the mayor and to the chief of police that they can rely upon. That is very important. This is the start of a new process here for the city. I think that we are all looking forward to seeing what imperfections might be there in this process that we can work on going forward. I hope we are all very open-minded individuals about what that is. And I appreciate that each and every one of you have agreed to participate in this process, understanding what that process looks like. And with that, I am going to ask if anybody has any questions.
